Now Hera, don't fly into such a rage at fellow gods. These two can never attain the same degree of honor. Still, the immortals love Prince Hector dearly. Best of all the mortals born in Troy. So I loved him at least. He never sinned with gifts to please my heart. Never once did my altar lack its share of victims. Wine, caps tipped and a deep smoky savior. These are the gifts we claim. These are our rights. But as for sealing courageous Hector's body, we must abandon the idea and not a chance in the world behind Achilles back. For fetus is always there, his mother always hovering near him night and day.

Achilles must receive a ransom from King Pyam. Achilles must give Hector's body back. Okay, does that make sense? So the gods are fighting over what to do. And then Zeus says, "You know what? Let's just poke over a piece between Achilles and Pry." Okay, so Prime agrees to ransom back Hector's body, and Achilles agrees.

Prime cannot sleep and tosses in his bed. His wife and his children come one by one to console the weeping king, but to no avail. His servants try different sleeping potions and one by one they fail. In the middle of the night, he screams at the moon and tears at his graying hair. Prime aches for Hector and feels guilt and remorse for failing his son.

Children spies watch Achilles drag Hector's body day and night. They take turns spying and know that Achilles cannot sleep. They report this news to Prime, giving him hope. He sends an emissary to the Greek camp, and Agamemnon agrees that it is Prime's right to ransom back his son as a custom of war. Even after the rage of Achilles, Agamemnon sends a servant to talk with Achilles.

Achilles does not hear Prime's offer but nods his head anyway. So, it's less powerful, less truthful, and less interesting. Now comes the most powerful part of the iliac. This is actually when Pry and Achilles meet for the first time. And so what happens is that Prime is snuck into the tent by Hermes and the majestic king of Troy slips past the rest, kneeling down beside Achilles, claps his knees, and kisses his hands—those terrible men-killing hands that have slaughtered Prime's many sons in battle.

So the king has an opportunity to kill Achilles but chooses instead to kiss his hand and submit before Achilles. This submission destroys the pride of Achilles. As when the group of madness seizes one who murders a man in his own fatherland and flees abroad to foreign shores to a wealthy noble host, a sense of marvel runs through all who see him. Soles marvel beholding majestic Pry. Prime is like a fugitive who's wanted for murder but escapes and becomes wealthy.

By submitting himself before Achilles, Prime has changed the destiny of the world. His men marveled too, with startled glances, but Prime prayed his heart out to Achilles: Remember your own father, great God, as old as I am, pass a threshold of deadly old age. Now doubt the countrymen round about him plague him now with no one there to defend him beat away disaster. No one but at least he hears you're still alive and his old heart rejoices, hopes rising day by day to see his beloved son come selling home from Troy.

Those words stir within Achilles a deep desire to grieve for his own father. Taking the old man's hand, he gently moves him back, overpowered by memory. Both men give way to grief. Prime weeps freely for man-killing Hector, probably encroaching before Achilles' feet as Achilles weeps for himself. This is the first time Achilles can now cry. Now for his father, now for Petraus once again, and they sobbing roles fall throughout the house. They forgive each other because they love their people. Prime saw Hector in the face of Achilles, and Achilles saw his father in the face of Pry. Because of their love for others, they find love for each other.

Love is the unifying force of the universe. Love allows us to forgive ourselves and others.
